title: COBALT: Contextual Bandit Learning with Offline Trajectories for Multi-Turn Code Generation
authors: Ziru Chen; Dongdong Chen; Ruinan Jin; Yingbin Liang; Yujia Xie; Huan Sun
source_note: The arXiv v2 title and October 2026 TMLR index agree on COBALT; an earlier title and OpenReview record belong to an earlier version.
access_depth: Primary v2 metadata/abstract and TMLR publication index; parent researcher inspected v1 misleading-feedback analysis, §§5.1–5.4; v2 HTML unavailable
contribution: Trains multi-turn code generation from offline partial trajectories using a contextual-bandit objective.
key_findings: The reported method improves code-generation performance and includes a perturbation experiment in which misleading execution feedback can degrade otherwise correct code.
importance: This is the closest direct precedent against claiming that wrong feedback undoing a fix is itself new.
relevance: The manuscript's false-FAIL fork changes a verdict after a verified candidate; COBALT corrupts public-test feedback in general coding.
transferable_idea: Measure security and functionality separately, manipulate feedback reliability, and test whether independent evidence prevents harmful revisions.
limitations: The security-specific mechanism and transport across task families remain to be demonstrated; original experiments are not replications of the manuscript.

title: AgentAbstain: Do LLM Agents Know When Not to Act?
authors: Xun Liu; Yi Evie Zhang; Vira Kasprova; Parisa Rabbani; Pardis Sadat Zahraei; Tianyu Zhang; Ali Ebrahimpour-Boroojeny; Varun Chandrasekaran
source_note: NeurIPS 2026 official downloads list the paper; the project identifies the Evaluations & Datasets track. Full text inspected for paired tasks and evaluation.
access_depth: Primary abstract plus targeted full-text methods/results inspection; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Introduces paired executable tasks that distinguish appropriate action from appropriate abstention.
key_findings: Across 263 task pairs and 42 environments, the best reported paired accuracy is 59.5%; task competence does not reliably predict restraint.
importance: It establishes abstention as an existing agent-evaluation target and operationalizes errors before and during execution.
relevance: The manuscript's impossible-task and stopping questions overlap directly, but secure-onset feedback manipulation is a different intervention.
transferable_idea: Borrow minimally changed task pairs, commit-level behavioral evidence, explicit over-abstention controls, and human task validation.
limitations: The benchmark combines deterministic traces and an LLM response judge; informational tasks rely on judged answers. It does not prove a universal impossibility oracle.

title: Coding Agents Don't Know When to Act
authors: Thibaud Gloaguen; Niels Mündler; Mark Müller; Veselin Raychev; Martin Vechev
source_note: No reviewed venue was verified. FixedBench is the benchmark name in this preprint; introductory methodology and reproduction-first caveat inspected.
access_depth: Primary abstract plus targeted full-text methods/results inspection; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Constructs FixedBench from resolved software issues to test whether coding agents avoid unnecessary changes.
key_findings: Models often modify already-fixed code; reproduction-first instructions reduce this but can induce premature abstention on partially fixed issues.
importance: It supplies a realistic action-bias baseline and shows that instructions can move both sides of an action boundary.
relevance: The manuscript's truthful-PASS regressions may reflect continuation pressure rather than a false-feedback effect.
transferable_idea: Add already-correct and partially-correct controls, vary continuation wording, and count harmful edits alongside necessary repairs.
limitations: Undesirable modifications are not all security regressions; the preprint's repositories and harnesses differ from finite-mode tasks.

title: Hell or High Water: Evaluating Agentic Recovery from External Failures
authors: Andrew Wang; Sophia Hager; Adi Asija; Daniel Khashabi; Nicholas Andrews
source_note: arXiv author comment identifies COLM 2025 acceptance.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Evaluates recovery when functions fail while alternative solutions are guaranteed to remain available.
key_findings: Agents frequently fail to find backup plans even when the action search space is restricted.
importance: It separates environmental failure from actual unsolvability, a distinction the historical hidden-veto condition failed to preserve.
relevance: The manuscript can contrast persistent search on genuinely impossible tasks with justified persistence on repairable tasks after tool failure.
transferable_idea: Construct matched recoverable failures and proven bounded impossibilities, with equivalent budgets and feedback detail.
limitations: Planning failures do not directly establish security repair behavior; its guarantee concerns the authored planning environment rather than arbitrary software.

title: Do LLMs Catch Their Own Mistakes? A Comprehensive Benchmark for Reflective Tool Use LLMs
authors: Zheyuan Liu; Liqiang Xiao; Yang Li; Hyokun Yun; Lihong Li; Chao Zhang; Meng Jiang
source_note: ACL Anthology confirms Findings of ACL 2026 and the complete author list.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Introduces ReflecTool-Bench for detecting and correcting tool-use mistakes in multi-turn dialogues.
key_findings: The benchmark spans 968 dialogues, 88 APIs and ten domains; models perform worse on their own errors than on third-party critique.
importance: It shows why recognizing another agent's defect and repairing one's own trajectory are distinct capabilities.
relevance: The manuscript's source-feature counts do not establish error recognition or semantic adaptation, which this benchmark measures explicitly.
transferable_idea: Separate detection, classification, correction and explanation; compare self-generated secure candidates with externally supplied matched candidates.
limitations: Dialogue annotation and injected errors are not equivalent to executed security-property checks. Explainability scores do not expose private reasoning.

title: When May an Agent Stop? Evidence-Carrying Termination for Tool-Using LLMs
authors: Jason Liu
source_note: Only an arXiv preprint was verified; do not imply peer review.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Proposes evidence-carrying termination: completion requires a typed certificate linked to scoped trace evidence and deterministic replay.
key_findings: The reported synthetic and prospective trajectory studies reduce unsupported completions while preserving much supported completion.
importance: It provides a close antecedent to requiring receipts before an agent can stop successfully.
relevance: The manuscript's parser-induced termination labels motivate separating a requested stop, controller acceptance and evidence-supported completion.
transferable_idea: Implement an explicit state machine and compare certificate-gated stopping with natural-language stopping under matched task states.
limitations: The certificate proves support in a declared trace, not external truth or security. It remains a preprint evaluated in controlled environments.

title: From Confident Closing to Silent Failure: Characterizing False Success in LLM Agents
authors: Laksh Advani
source_note: The arXiv author record states acceptance to FAGEN at ICML 2026; this is a workshop paper, not an ICML main-conference paper.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Measures false success by comparing agents' completion claims with independently recorded environment state.
key_findings: Across tau2-bench and AppWorld, false-success frequency varies strongly by setting; the tested LLM judges often fail to distinguish it.
importance: It warns against using confident language or trace volume as substitutes for validated outcomes.
relevance: The manuscript's recovered 0/15 unsupported claims are conditional on its narrow checker and cannot establish low false-success risk.
transferable_idea: Preserve explicit claim missingness and score claims against independent security and functional outcomes.
limitations: Workshop evidence is domain-specific; lightweight classifiers are triage signals, and their detection performance should not be transferred numerically.

title: From Dead Code and Static Requirements to Working Engines: Software Revival with Coding Agents
authors: Tianyu Liu; Dingyuan Dai; Yufan Du; Zhen Yang
source_note: Full-text verifier audit inspected, especially §8; no peer-reviewed venue was verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract plus targeted full-text methods/results inspection; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Introduces software revival and engine-reconstruction tasks and audits their hidden verifiers.
key_findings: The authors identify 28 verifier defects, including 24 false negatives, and retract a solver-capability interpretation exposed by a minimal passing counterexample.
importance: It already makes verifier validation, attainable specifications and self-reported diagnostics central scientific issues.
relevance: The hidden-veto audit is a concrete local instance of a broader, already documented construct-validity problem.
transferable_idea: Add hand-derived oracle self-tests, achievability probes and independent candidate comparisons; recompute properties from submitted artifacts.
limitations: Candidate consensus is an anomaly signal, not truth. The small task suite does not estimate general benchmark defect prevalence.

title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
authors: Shunyu Yao; Jeffrey Zhao; Dian Yu; Nan Du; Izhak Shafran; Karthik Narasimhan; Yuan Cao
source_note: arXiv describes its version as the ICLR camera-ready paper.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Interleaves language-model reasoning and actions so environmental observations can inform subsequent decisions.
key_findings: It improves performance over selected baselines on question answering, fact checking and interactive decision tasks.
importance: It is a foundational design for the observation–action loops used by modern coding agents.
relevance: The manuscript examines what happens when an observation in such a loop is invalid or cannot justify its advertised meaning.
transferable_idea: Treat feedback as a manipulable input and record the exact observation available before every action.
limitations: Reported text traces are not guaranteed faithful explanations of internal computation; success in these environments does not establish security competence.

title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
authors: Noah Shinn; Federico Cassano; Ashwin Gopinath; Karthik Narasimhan; Shunyu Yao
source_note: NeurIPS publication has five authors; later arXiv version adds Edward Berman. This entry uses the published author list.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Uses verbal reflection stored in episodic memory to improve later attempts without changing model weights.
key_findings: The paper reports gains across decision-making, coding and reasoning, with sensitivity to feedback sources and memory design.
importance: It established a reusable architecture in which evaluations affect future behavior through language rather than gradients.
relevance: Wrong checker messages could contaminate a reflection memory and affect more than the immediate next candidate.
transferable_idea: Compare ephemeral feedback with persistent reflection memory, tracking whether an independently corrected verdict removes later errors.
limitations: The original positive results do not establish robustness to faulty judges, and verbal reflections cannot be treated as ground-truth causal mechanisms.

title: Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
authors: Aman Madaan; Niket Tandon; Prakhar Gupta; Skyler Hallinan; Luyu Gao; Sarah Wiegreffe; Uri Alon; Nouha Dziri; Shrimai Prabhumoye; Yiming Yang; Shashank Gupta; Bodhisattwa Prasad Majumder; Katherine Hermann; Sean Welleck; Amir Yazdanbakhsh; Peter Clark
source_note: NeurIPS 2023 primary proceedings record verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Uses one language model to generate an answer, critique it and iteratively revise it without additional model training.
key_findings: The authors report improvements across seven tasks, including code and reasoning, relative to single-pass generation.
importance: It established feedback-driven refinement as a general inference-time technique rather than a special-purpose repair pipeline.
relevance: The manuscript must explain why extra iteration sometimes destroys correctness instead of assuming self-correction should always help.
transferable_idea: Compare revision with resampling and a no-edit control at equal inference budgets; track transitions from correct to incorrect as well as the reverse.
limitations: The feedback is model-generated and task-dependent. Positive aggregate results do not establish safety when external verdicts are wrong.

title: CRITIC: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing
authors: Zhibin Gou; Zhihong Shao; Yeyun Gong; Yelong Shen; Yujiu Yang; Nan Duan; Weizhu Chen
source_note: arXiv author record identifies ICLR 2024.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Uses external tools to critique and revise model answers through an interactive validation loop.
key_findings: Reported gains span question answering, mathematical program synthesis and toxicity reduction; the paper emphasizes the value of external feedback.
importance: It helps separate intrinsic self-critique from correction supported by new environmental evidence.
relevance: The manuscript concerns an important boundary condition: external feedback is useful only to the extent its semantics and implementation are valid.
transferable_idea: Vary whether feedback contains a bare label, a reproducible failing case or an independent checker disagreement, while holding correction opportunities fixed.
limitations: The evaluated tools are not adversarial security oracles; the reported improvements do not predict robustness to systematically misleading tests.

title: Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
authors: Xinyun Chen; Maxwell Lin; Nathanael Schärli; Denny Zhou
source_note: ICLR 2024 primary OpenReview PDF verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Teaches models to inspect generated programs, execution outcomes and natural-language explanations to debug their own code.
key_findings: Few-shot self-debugging improves code generation across several settings, including tasks without explicit correctness tests and tasks with unit-test feedback.
importance: It provides a concrete precedent for reusing a candidate and its execution history instead of repeatedly sampling from scratch.
relevance: The manuscript can test whether explanation-supported debugging protects correct security code or merely rationalizes an incorrect verdict.
transferable_idea: Compare code explanation, raw execution evidence and label-only feedback; score candidate preservation independently of explanation fluency.
limitations: Rubber-duck explanations are observable outputs, not verified accounts of model reasoning. Benchmark unit tests do not establish comprehensive program correctness.

title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
authors: Jie Huang; Xinyun Chen; Swaroop Mishra; Huaixiu Steven Zheng; Adams Wei Yu; Xinying Song; Denny Zhou
source_note: arXiv author record identifies ICLR 2024.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Systematically tests whether language models can improve reasoning through intrinsic self-correction without external evidence.
key_findings: The examined models often fail to improve and can replace correct answers with incorrect ones under self-correction prompts.
importance: It is an influential counterweight to treating iteration or confidence as a generally reliable corrective mechanism.
relevance: The manuscript's truthful-PASS regressions require a correction-pressure control even before attributing additional damage to false feedback.
transferable_idea: Factor continuation prompts separately from verdict truth, and retain the initial correct answer as an explicit no-change option.
limitations: The scope is intrinsic reasoning correction in particular models and tasks; the result does not imply that informative external feedback cannot help.

title: Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning
authors: Aviral Kumar; Vincent Zhuang; Rishabh Agarwal; Yi Su; John D Co-Reyes; Avi Singh; Kate Baumli; Shariq Iqbal; Colton Bishop; Rebecca Roelofs; Lei M Zhang; Kay McKinney; Disha Shrivastava; Cosmin Paduraru; George Tucker; Doina Precup; Feryal Behbahani; Aleksandra Faust
source_note: ICLR 2025 primary OpenReview PDF verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Trains multi-turn self-correction through reinforcement learning on the model's own evolving outputs.
key_findings: The authors report improvements on mathematical reasoning and code generation and identify distribution mismatch and behavior collapse as problems for simpler training alternatives.
importance: It shows that correction competence depends on training and trajectory distribution, not just an instruction to reconsider.
relevance: A single small model cannot establish a general law of agent behavior under misleading feedback.
transferable_idea: Compare models with documented correction training, and train a policy to preserve independently verified properties while deciding whether further edits are worthwhile.
limitations: The paper studies correctness-oriented rewards; security preservation under unreliable evaluators remains a separate empirical question.

title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
authors: Carlos E. Jimenez; John Yang; Alexander Wettig; Shunyu Yao; Kexin Pei; Ofir Press; Karthik Narasimhan
source_note: arXiv author record identifies ICLR 2024.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Creates an executable benchmark from real GitHub issues paired with repository snapshots and associated tests.
key_findings: The original release contains 2,294 issues from twelve Python repositories and shows that repository-level issue resolution is substantially harder than isolated function generation.
importance: It grounds software-agent evaluation in actual maintenance contexts and reproducible code execution.
relevance: The manuscript's finite modes offer controlled mechanisms but need external validation on tasks with realistic dependencies and partial specifications.
transferable_idea: Add a small, carefully audited repository-level repair set, retaining both regression tests and independent security properties.
limitations: Issue-linked tests encode only part of intent, and benchmark success cannot by itself establish complete correctness, maintainability or security.

title: SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
authors: John Yang; Carlos E. Jimenez; Alexander Wettig; Kilian Lieret; Shunyu Yao; Karthik Narasimhan; Ofir Press
source_note: NeurIPS 2024 primary proceedings record verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Designs an agent-computer interface tailored to repository navigation, editing and execution.
key_findings: The reported agent solves real software issues, and interface choices materially affect its ability to operate in coding environments.
importance: It establishes scaffolding as an experimental factor rather than a neutral wrapper around a model.
relevance: The manuscript's parser reminders and adapter-induced stops could explain behavior attributed to the agent.
transferable_idea: Publish the action grammar, exact tool receipts and controller state transitions; compare at least one standard agent interface with the custom adapter.
limitations: Performance claims are specific to the evaluated models, interface and benchmark version; they do not isolate reasoning ability from orchestration quality.

title: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
authors: Chunqiu Steven Xia; Yinlin Deng; Soren Dunn; Lingming Zhang
source_note: FSE 2025 official program verifies the published title Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents; Agentless is the preprint/system name.
venue: FSE 2025 / Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Builds Agentless, a scripted localization, repair and validation pipeline, to examine whether complex software-agent interaction is necessary.
key_findings: The paper reports competitive issue-resolution performance and identifies benchmark cases with misleading descriptions or information leakage.
importance: It challenges assumptions that more autonomy, dialogue or architectural complexity necessarily improves repair.
relevance: The manuscript's elaborate action loop needs a simple repair-and-validate baseline to show what sequential decision-making contributes.
transferable_idea: Compare a bounded one-shot repair, scripted generate-test selection and an interactive agent under matched cost and checker access.
limitations: Published results concern selected repository tasks and models; a simpler pipeline may still lack capabilities needed for ambiguous or genuinely interactive security work.

title: AgentBoard: An Analytical Evaluation Board of Multi-turn LLM Agents
authors: Chang Ma; Junlei Zhang; Zhihao Zhu; Cheng Yang; Yujiu Yang; Yaohui Jin; Zhenzhong Lan; Lingpeng Kong; Junxian He
source_note: arXiv author record identifies NeurIPS 2024.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Provides a common framework for evaluating multi-turn agents with detailed measures of intermediate task progress.
key_findings: Fine-grained analyses expose differences that final success rates conceal across interactive tasks and models.
importance: It demonstrates that an agent can fail overall after making meaningful progress, or appear active without advancing toward the objective.
relevance: The manuscript's action counts and final labels cannot identify when a valid fix was reached or when it was damaged.
transferable_idea: Record per-step security and functionality states, then summarize first success, preservation duration, regression and recovery.
limitations: Progress measures still depend on valid task-specific definitions; adding intermediate metrics does not repair a faulty acceptance rule.

title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
authors: Xiao Liu; Hao Yu; Hanchen Zhang; Yifan Xu; Xuanyu Lei; Hanyu Lai; Yu Gu; Hangliang Ding; Kaiwen Men; Kejuan Yang; Shudan Zhang; Xiang Deng; Aohan Zeng; Zhengxiao Du; Chenhui Zhang; Sheng Shen; Tianjun Zhang; Yu Su; Huan Sun; Minlie Huang; Yuxiao Dong; Jie Tang
source_note: arXiv author record identifies ICLR 2024.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Benchmarks language models as agents across eight interactive environments with heterogeneous actions and goals.
key_findings: The analysis reveals substantial capability gaps and recurring failures in planning and instruction following across models.
importance: It supplies broad evidence that agent performance is strongly environment- and task-dependent.
relevance: The manuscript's five small security task families and one primary model cannot support universal conclusions about autonomous agents.
transferable_idea: Treat family and model as explicit dimensions, report within-family transitions and compare general tool competence with secure-repair behavior.
limitations: Cross-environment aggregate scores can hide very different failure mechanisms, and the benchmark does not establish security-specific causal explanations.

title: WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents
authors: Shuyan Zhou; Frank F. Xu; Hao Zhu; Xuhui Zhou; Robert Lo; Abishek Sridhar; Xianyi Cheng; Tianyue Ou; Yonatan Bisk; Daniel Fried; Uri Alon; Graham Neubig
source_note: ICLR 2024 primary OpenReview PDF verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Creates realistic, reproducible web environments with tasks evaluated through their functional outcomes.
key_findings: The original experiments reveal a large gap between autonomous agents and human performance on long, compositional web tasks.
importance: It makes environment state, rather than a persuasive final answer, central to evaluating task accomplishment.
relevance: The manuscript likewise needs to distinguish verbal completion, public checker acceptance and independently measured program behavior.
transferable_idea: Maintain explicit snapshots of the environment and candidate at every verdict; define success from state transitions that match the intended task.
limitations: Realistic interfaces do not guarantee complete evaluators, and a web-task success predicate is not a transferable security oracle.

title: Who Verifies the Verifier? Co-Evolving Inspectable Graders with Self-Improving Agents
authors: Xing Zhang; Guanghui Wang; Yanwei Cui; Ziyuan Li; Wei Qiu; Bing Zhu; Peiyang He
source_note: arXiv identifies a NeurIPS 2026 workshop acceptance; full text inspected for anchor ablation, including §5.2.
venue: NeurIPS 2026 workshop Who Verifies the Agents? (accepted)
access_depth: Primary abstract plus targeted full-text methods/results inspection; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Co-evolves agent skills and inspectable graders built from typed, deterministic detectors with human-auditable logic.
key_findings: An ablation without anchor safeguards produces nearly always-passing graders even while downstream agent improvements remain comparable.
importance: It demonstrates that improved agent scores cannot validate the quality of the verifier used during development.
relevance: The manuscript's hidden veto is the opposite degenerate rule: an evaluator can be systematically wrong while retaining plausible surface behavior.
transferable_idea: Reserve independent anchor cases unseen during verifier selection and evaluate agent quality and verifier discrimination separately.
limitations: The experiments use small anchor sets and gains vary by benchmark; inspectability and anchor consistency do not establish complete semantic correctness.

title: Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction? Measuring Verification Transport for LLM Agent Evaluation
authors: Disha Sheshanarayana; Sai Linisha Reddy Goli
source_note: Submitted November 13, 2026 and therefore within cutoff. Workshop acceptance per arXiv; full-text methods and conditional denominator inspected.
venue: NeurIPS 2026 workshop Who Verifies the Agents? (accepted)
access_depth: Primary abstract plus targeted full-text methods/results inspection; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Studies whether fixed verifier judgments remain valid when a completed trajectory is abstracted, delegated or compacted.
key_findings: Holding realized behavior and truth fixed, the paper finds failures under reduced observability and substantial recovery when provenance is restored.
importance: It isolates the evidence representation as a cause of evaluation failure, separate from the underlying agent's competence.
relevance: The manuscript's incomplete receipts and adapter summaries can change what an observer is justified in concluding.
transferable_idea: Run matched full-trace, summarized-trace and provenance-restored evaluation, separating wrong verdicts from missing verdicts.
limitations: The transport denominator conditions on native correct judgments, so native accuracy must also be reported; restored evidence cannot fix an intrinsically wrong specification.

title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
authors: Shunyu Yao; Noah Shinn; Pedram Razavi; Karthik Narasimhan
source_note: ICLR 2025 primary OpenReview PDF verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Evaluates tool-using agents interacting with simulated users while following domain policies.
key_findings: Final database states and repeated-trial consistency expose unreliable behavior that single successful conversations can conceal.
importance: It adds policy compliance and reproducibility to ordinary task completion, with a pass-to-the-k style consistency measure.
relevance: The manuscript's few episodes per condition cannot reveal whether apparent secure repair is stable across repeated runs.
transferable_idea: Use state-based outcome checks, explicit policy constraints and repeated paired continuations with transparent denominators.
limitations: Simulated user behavior and benchmark policies limit ecological validity; passing a finite task set does not certify broader security or reliability.

title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
authors: Timo Schick; Jane Dwivedi-Yu; Roberto Dessì; Roberta Raileanu; Maria Lomeli; Luke Zettlemoyer; Nicola Cancedda; Thomas Scialom
source_note: NeurIPS 2023 primary proceedings record verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Trains language models to decide when to invoke APIs, which API to use and how to incorporate the result.
key_findings: Self-supervised augmentation improves selected tasks using tools such as calculators, search and translation with limited demonstrations.
importance: It established tool selection and tool-result integration as trainable capabilities.
relevance: The manuscript should distinguish failure to choose a helpful check from failure to interpret a misleading check already provided.
transferable_idea: Log the available tool set and separate verification selection, observation interpretation and subsequent repair decisions.
limitations: External tools are generally treated as useful sources of information; the paper does not evaluate security invariants under corrupted execution feedback.

title: ToolLLM: Facilitating Large Language Models to Master 16000+ Real-world APIs
authors: Yujia Qin; Shihao Liang; Yining Ye; Kunlun Zhu; Lan Yan; Yaxi Lu; Yankai Lin; Xin Cong; Xiangru Tang; Bill Qian; Sihan Zhao; Lauren Hong; Runchu Tian; Ruobing Xie; Jie Zhou; Mark Gerstein; Dahai Li; Zhiyuan Liu; Maosong Sun
source_note: ICLR 2024 primary OpenReview PDF verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Builds a large API instruction corpus and tool-use system with retrieval, model tuning and search over action paths.
key_findings: The paper reports stronger generalization across API-oriented tasks using data covering more than sixteen thousand real-world APIs.
importance: It connects tool discovery with planning when the available action space is too large to place directly in context.
relevance: The manuscript's fixed guidance injection and tiny tool set are much narrower than genuine retrieval-assisted tool use.
transferable_idea: If retrieval becomes a contribution, evaluate query-dependent document or tool selection, relevance failures and the evidence actually used.
limitations: API availability and generated training instructions can change; benchmark preference judgments do not substitute for validated security outcomes.

title: Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks
authors: Daoan Zhang; Qinbo Bai; Dehai Min; Xingyu Mu; Ziyi Chen; Jianing Yin
source_note: Submitted November 9, 2026 and therefore within cutoff; preprint. Full-text §4.5 inspected for verdict delivery and error direction.
access_depth: Primary abstract plus targeted full-text methods/results inspection; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Generates task verifiers through a harness combining evidence, authoring instructions and multiple verification modalities.
key_findings: Comparisons reveal over-strict generated checks, overly lenient official checks and substantial differences between verdict accuracy and verdict delivery.
importance: It treats verifier construction as an engineering problem with measurable failure modes, rather than assuming an official checker is authoritative.
relevance: The manuscript's missing receipts and hidden rejection rule require both delivery accounting and independent semantic validation.
transferable_idea: Benchmark a checker against deliberately correct, unsafe, overblocking and invalid candidates; include an explicit no-verdict state.
limitations: Evaluation still depends on constructed candidate sets and reference labels. Better agreement on this set cannot prove that unknown security defects are excluded.

title: Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox
authors: Yangjun Ruan; Honghua Dong; Andrew Wang; Silviu Pitis; Yongchao Zhou; Jimmy Ba; Yann Dubois; Chris J. Maddison; Tatsunori Hashimoto
source_note: ICLR 2024 primary OpenReview PDF verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Uses a language model to emulate tool environments and another evaluation process to identify risky agent behavior.
key_findings: The experiments uncover potential failures at reduced evaluation cost, with human review confirming only a subset as realistic and valid.
importance: It offers a scalable way to generate adversarial situations while exposing the need to validate synthetic findings.
relevance: The manuscript's hand-designed security modes can serve as exploratory probes, but their semantics require independent checking before broad interpretation.
transferable_idea: Use model-generated scenarios to discover candidate failure modes, then reproduce them in executable environments and blind human audits.
limitations: An emulated environment can invent or misrepresent tool behavior; risk judgments from the emulator are not ground-truth evidence.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
authors: Patrick Lewis; Ethan Perez; Aleksandra Piktus; Fabio Petroni; Vladimir Karpukhin; Naman Goyal; Heinrich Küttler; Mike Lewis; Wen-tau Yih; Tim Rocktäschel; Sebastian Riedel; Douwe Kiela
source_note: arXiv author record identifies NeurIPS 2020.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Combines a pretrained generator with retrieval from an external document index for knowledge-intensive language tasks.
key_findings: The reported approach improves selected knowledge tasks and produces more factual, specific outputs than purely parametric comparison models.
importance: It is the foundational reference for distinguishing retrieval-augmented inference from merely inserting a fixed guide.
relevance: The manuscript's static guidance condition should not inherit claims about retrieval quality or document selection that it never tests.
transferable_idea: Introduce query-dependent retrieval only if the scientific question requires it; record relevance, provenance and conflicting evidence separately from repair success.
limitations: Knowledge retrieval does not validate executable behavior, and retrieved documents may be outdated, irrelevant or inconsistent with the current program.

title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
authors: Akari Asai; Zeqiu Wu; Yizhong Wang; Avirup Sil; Hannaneh Hajishirzi
source_note: ICLR 2024 primary OpenReview PDF verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Learns when to retrieve and how to critique retrieved information and generated answers using reflection tokens.
key_findings: The paper reports improvements in factuality and citation-related evaluation while avoiding unnecessary retrieval on some inputs.
importance: It connects information acquisition with judgments of evidential usefulness rather than treating every retrieval as beneficial.
relevance: The manuscript could distinguish harmful verdict obedience from a failure to obtain or use independent security evidence.
transferable_idea: Compare always-retrieve, never-retrieve and evidence-triggered retrieval, with independent grading of whether retrieved material supports the proposed edit.
limitations: Reflection scores are learned signals, not proofs. Gains in knowledge tasks do not establish calibrated trust in code checkers.

title: Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation
authors: Shi-Qi Yan; Jia-Chen Gu; Yun Zhu; Zhen-Hua Ling
source_note: ACL Anthology confirms an expanded Findings of IJCNLP-AACL 2026 publication; the older 2024 preprint is not counted separately.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: The expanded published version orchestrates corrective retrieval through an agent choosing internal retrieval, web search and several relevance evaluators.
key_findings: Experiments across five datasets report improved generation accuracy and efficiency compared with the evaluated retrieval baselines.
importance: It treats retrieved evidence as potentially inadequate and provides mechanisms for changing the information source.
relevance: The manuscript currently tests fixed guidance; a meaningful retrieval extension would need to detect when available security guidance cannot resolve a checker disagreement.
transferable_idea: Compare a relevance evaluator with an independent executable counterexample, measuring whether either changes the agent's decision to edit.
limitations: This entry describes the 2026 publication, not just the shorter 2024 preprint; retrieval correctness is distinct from program or security correctness.

title: Active Retrieval Augmented Generation
authors: Zhengbao Jiang; Frank F. Xu; Luyu Gao; Zhiqing Sun; Qian Liu; Jane Dwivedi-Yu; Yiming Yang; Jamie Callan; Graham Neubig
source_note: arXiv author record identifies EMNLP 2023.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Triggers retrieval during generation by anticipating the next content and detecting low-confidence material.
key_findings: The reported FLARE method improves several long-form generation tasks compared with evaluated retrieval strategies.
importance: It makes information acquisition an adaptive action within a trajectory, rather than a single preparatory step.
relevance: The manuscript's agents may need additional evidence only when verdicts conflict with observed behavior.
transferable_idea: Test an uncertainty-triggered evidence request against fixed retrieval frequency, matching total retrieval and generation budgets.
limitations: Token uncertainty is an imperfect proxy for semantic uncertainty. The original evaluations concern text generation, so any benefit for security repair remains a hypothesis requiring new experiments.

title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
authors: Nelson F. Liu; Kevin Lin; John Hewitt; Ashwin Paranjape; Michele Bevilacqua; Fabio Petroni; Percy Liang
source_note: Official TACL PDF confirms publication in February 2024, volume 12, pages 157–173, despite acceptance in 2023.
venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Measures how the location of relevant information within long contexts affects model performance.
key_findings: On document question answering and key-value retrieval, relevant information is often used better near context boundaries than in the middle.
importance: It demonstrates that receiving evidence and reliably using it are different capabilities.
relevance: The manuscript's growing action traces may bury an earlier passing candidate or an important security constraint.
transferable_idea: Randomize the position of invariant reminders and verified receipts, or preserve them in a compact structured state, without changing their content.
limitations: The experiments involve particular models and retrieval tasks; an effect in repair must be measured rather than assumed from context length alone.

title: RepoCoder: Repository-Level Code Completion Through Iterative Retrieval and Generation
authors: Fengji Zhang; Bei Chen; Yue Zhang; Jacky Keung; Jin Liu; Daoguang Zan; Yi Mao; Jian-Guang Lou; Weizhu Chen
source_note: arXiv author record identifies EMNLP 2023 main conference.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Alternates repository-level retrieval and code generation to improve completion using related project code.
key_findings: The method outperforms evaluated retrieval-free and simpler retrieval baselines on repository completion at several granularities.
importance: It shows how an initially generated candidate can improve the next retrieval query and subsequent code context.
relevance: The manuscript's fixed guide lacks this adaptive coupling between current candidate and retrieved evidence.
transferable_idea: Retrieve nearby security checks and their tests after each proposed edit, then assess whether this preserves project-specific invariants.
limitations: Completion quality differs from repair correctness, and similar repository code can reproduce an existing vulnerability or outdated convention.

title: CodePlan: Repository-level Coding using LLMs and Planning
authors: Ramakrishna Bairi; Atharv Sonwane; Aditya Kanade; Vageesh D C; Arun Iyer; Suresh Parthasarathy; Sriram Rajamani; B. Ashok; Shashank Shet
source_note: FSE 2024 official program verifies the paper; arXiv provides metadata and abstract.
venue: FSE 2024 / Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Treats repository-wide modification as planning over dependencies and the effects of previous edits.
key_findings: The reported system better completes multi-file migration and change tasks than baselines without an effective plan.
importance: It explains why local code validity can be insufficient when a change affects dependent files or assumptions.
relevance: The manuscript's bounded modes simplify away cross-file security consequences that a stronger external evaluation should expose.
transferable_idea: Add tasks where key rotation or authorization changes require coordinated updates, recording dependency breakage separately from local test success.
limitations: The evaluated transformations are not equivalent to adversarial vulnerability repair, and plans remain dependent on the quality of dependency analysis and validation.

title: InterCode: Standardizing and Benchmarking Interactive Coding with Execution Feedback
authors: John Yang; Akshara Prabhakar; Karthik Narasimhan; Shunyu Yao
source_note: NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks primary proceedings verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Standardizes interactive coding environments in which programs are actions and execution results provide observations.
key_findings: The benchmark enables controlled comparison of iterative code-producing agents across executable task settings.
importance: It supplies reusable experimental structure for studying how successive observations influence code actions.
relevance: The manuscript similarly needs exact action–observation records, reproducible environments and clear distinction between raw execution and rewritten feedback.
transferable_idea: Implement feedback interventions at a documented observation boundary while retaining an untouched execution record for independent evaluation.
limitations: Interactive execution creates evidence but does not guarantee the evaluator matches task intent; corruption of the wrapper must be separated from runtime failure.

title: CodeRL: Mastering Code Generation through Pretrained Models and Deep Reinforcement Learning
authors: Hung Le; Yue Wang; Akhilesh Deepak Gotmare; Silvio Savarese; Steven C.H. Hoi
source_note: arXiv notes that an earlier version was accepted at NeurIPS 2022; annotation concerns the paper's central method, not a new publication.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Combines pretrained code generation with reinforcement learning and a critic trained to predict functional correctness.
key_findings: The paper reports improved programming performance using execution-based rewards and critic-guided generation and refinement.
importance: It makes test feedback influential both during learning and during candidate selection.
relevance: The manuscript's hidden veto illustrates how an incorrect reward or verdict can invalidate a claimed correction objective.
transferable_idea: Compare a frozen generator with a feedback-trained model, and audit whether evaluator corruption changes learned or immediate editing behavior.
limitations: Unit-test reward is an approximation to correctness. Security claims require properties and negative cases beyond the original functional programming tasks.

title: LEVER: Learning to Verify Language-to-Code Generation with Execution
authors: Ansong Ni; Srini Iyer; Dragomir Radev; Veselin Stoyanov; Wen-Tau Yih; Sida Wang; Xi Victoria Lin
source_note: ICML 2023 PMLR publication verified; author names use the official proceedings form.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Trains an execution-aware verifier to score generated programs using the input, source code and observed outputs.
key_findings: Reranking with verification scores improves performance across four language-to-code datasets in the reported experiments.
importance: It shows that executable evidence can be interpreted jointly with program semantics rather than reduced to a single pass/fail bit.
relevance: The manuscript can compare bare checker labels with richer records that allow the agent to identify a contradictory verdict.
transferable_idea: Provide independently computed outputs and relevant source features, then test whether a verifier distinguishes unsafe acceptance from benign failure.
limitations: A learned verifier is another fallible model; reranking gains do not establish calibrated security judgments or coverage of rare vulnerabilities.

title: CodeT: Code Generation with Generated Tests
authors: Bei Chen; Fengji Zhang; Anh Nguyen; Daoguang Zan; Zeqi Lin; Jian-Guang Lou; Weizhu Chen
source_note: ICLR 2023 primary OpenReview PDF verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Generates tests alongside candidate programs and uses execution agreement to select solutions.
key_findings: The reported dual-execution agreement strategy improves code-generation accuracy on established programming benchmarks.
importance: It provides a concrete route to acquiring extra checks when a trusted test suite is unavailable.
relevance: The manuscript could ask whether independent tests reduce obedience to a false verdict or merely repeat the same mistaken specification.
transferable_idea: Compare same-model tests, independently authored tests and cross-model tests against a held-out security oracle.
limitations: Agreement can arise from shared errors; generated tests and candidate consensus must not become the definition of correctness in the evaluation.

title: Is Your Code Generated by ChatGPT Really Correct? Rigorous Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code Generation
authors: Jiawei Liu; Chunqiu Steven Xia; Yuyao Wang; Lingming Zhang
source_note: NeurIPS 2023 primary proceedings record verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Expands code-generation tests through model-assisted synthesis and mutation to probe solutions more rigorously.
key_findings: The expanded EvalPlus suites expose incorrect programs previously counted as correct and can alter model rankings.
importance: It directly demonstrates that finite evaluator coverage changes apparent capability.
relevance: The manuscript's raw-suite passes justify only a bounded property claim; stronger hidden tests may reveal additional unsafe or nonfunctional behavior.
transferable_idea: Build held-out tests from independent mechanisms and report original-suite, expanded-suite and security-property results separately.
limitations: More tests reduce some blind spots without proving semantic correctness, and test expansion can introduce its own invalid expectations.

title: LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code
authors: Naman Jain; King Han; Alex Gu; Wen-Ding Li; Fanjia Yan; Tianjun Zhang; Sida Wang; Armando Solar-Lezama; Koushik Sen; Ion Stoica
source_note: ICLR 2025 primary OpenReview PDF verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Uses temporally collected programming problems to evaluate generation, self-repair, execution and test-output prediction.
key_findings: The benchmark exposes variation across coding capabilities and offers release-time controls that reduce some contamination concerns.
importance: It separates producing code from understanding execution and responding to errors, which aggregate code scores can obscure.
relevance: The manuscript should measure whether an agent understands a failing case before interpreting its subsequent edit as corrective behavior.
transferable_idea: Add execution prediction and defect-localization probes alongside the repair task, with held-out problem dates when possible.
limitations: Temporal filtering cannot establish absolute absence of training contamination, and contest problems omit many deployment and security constraints.

title: BigCodeBench: Benchmarking Code Generation with Diverse Function Calls and Complex Instructions
authors: Terry Yue Zhuo; Minh Chien Vu; Jenny Chim; Han Hu; Wenhao Yu; Ratnadira Widyasari; Imam Nur Bani Yusuf; Haolan Zhan; Junda He; Indraneil Paul; Simon Brunner; Chen Gong; Thong Hoang; Armel Randy Zebaze; Xiaoheng Hong; Wen-Ding Li; Jean Kaddour; Ming Xu; Zhihan Zhang; Prateek Yadav; Naman Jain; Alex Gu; Zhoujun Cheng; Jiawei Liu; Qian Liu; Zijian Wang; Binyuan Hui; Niklas Muennighoff; David Lo; Daniel Fried; Xiaoning Du; Harm de Vries; Leandro Von Werra
source_note: arXiv author comment identifies ICLR 2025; inspected metadata version was available before the cutoff.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Evaluates code generation requiring diverse library calls and multi-step instructions.
key_findings: The benchmark contains 1,140 tasks covering 139 libraries and reports a persistent gap between evaluated models and human performance.
importance: It broadens evaluation beyond short algorithmic functions and makes interface composition part of correctness.
relevance: The manuscript's controlled security modes need follow-up tasks where library behavior and interactions can invalidate a superficially plausible fix.
transferable_idea: Include realistic cryptographic or request-processing libraries and evaluate normal workloads alongside exploit-blocking behavior.
limitations: High branch coverage describes test execution, not specification completeness or security assurance; dependency versions can also affect reproducibility.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code
authors: Mark Chen; Jerry Tworek; Heewoo Jun; Qiming Yuan; Henrique Ponde de Oliveira Pinto; Jared Kaplan; Harri Edwards; Yuri Burda; Nicholas Joseph; Greg Brockman; Alex Ray; Raul Puri; Gretchen Krueger; Michael Petrov; Heidy Khlaaf; Girish Sastry; Pamela Mishkin; Brooke Chan; Scott Gray; Nick Ryder; Mikhail Pavlov; Alethea Power; Lukasz Kaiser; Mohammad Bavarian; Clemens Winter; Philippe Tillet; Felipe Petroski Such; Dave Cummings; Matthias Plappert; Fotios Chantzis; Elizabeth Barnes; Ariel Herbert-Voss; William Hebgen Guss; Alex Nichol; Alex Paino; Nikolas Tezak; Jie Tang; Igor Babuschkin; Suchir Balaji; Shantanu Jain; William Saunders; Christopher Hesse; Andrew N. Carr; Jan Leike; Josh Achiam; Vedant Misra; Evan Morikawa; Alec Radford; Matthew Knight; Miles Brundage; Mira Murati; Katie Mayer; Peter Welinder; Bob McGrew; Dario Amodei; Sam McCandlish; Ilya Sutskever; Wojciech Zaremba
source_note: Technical-report preprint; no peer-reviewed venue is asserted.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Introduces Codex evaluations and the HumanEval benchmark for synthesizing functions from natural-language specifications.
key_findings: The report shows that sampling multiple candidates can substantially increase the availability of a test-passing solution.
importance: It made execution-based evaluation and pass-at-k central to modern code-generation research.
relevance: The manuscript should distinguish the existence of a correct candidate from the agent's ability to select and preserve it.
transferable_idea: Report initial-candidate correctness, best observed candidate and final selected candidate separately at matched sampling budgets.
limitations: This is a technical-report preprint. HumanEval tests cover finite functional behavior and do not validate security, deployment readiness or long-horizon agency.

title: SWE-Bench+: Enhanced Coding Benchmark for LLMs
authors: Reem Aleithan; Haoran Xue; Mohammad Mahdi Mohajer; Elijah Nnorom; Gias Uddin; Song Wang
source_note: No peer-reviewed venue was verified; audit claims refer to the selected successful-patch sample.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Audits SWE-bench results and proposes enhanced evaluation to address leakage and weak tests.
key_findings: Manual inspection of a selected set of successful agent patches finds substantial issue-description leakage and suspicious cases associated with inadequate validation.
importance: It challenges the assumption that a green benchmark result necessarily reflects genuine issue resolution.
relevance: The manuscript's checker audit should similarly connect a concrete implementation defect to the exact claims it invalidates.
transferable_idea: Blindly review passing and failing patches, preserve selection criteria, and report defect prevalence only for the audited sampling frame.
limitations: The quoted rates concern a selected successful-patch sample and should not be generalized to all SWE-bench tasks or all coding agents.

title: Competition-Level Code Generation with AlphaCode
authors: Yujia Li; David Choi; Junyoung Chung; Nate Kushman; Julian Schrittwieser; Rémi Leblond; Tom Eccles; James Keeling; Felix Gimeno; Agustin Dal Lago; Thomas Hubert; Peter Choy; Cyprien de Masson d'Autume; Igor Babuschkin; Xinyun Chen; Po-Sen Huang; Johannes Welbl; Sven Gowal; Alexey Cherepanov; James Molloy; Daniel J. Mankowitz; Esme Sutherland Robson; Pushmeet Kohli; Nando de Freitas; Koray Kavukcuoglu; Oriol Vinyals
source_note: arXiv record and Science DOI verify publication in 2022.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Combines large-scale code generation with filtering and clustering to solve competitive programming problems.
key_findings: The reported system reaches a competitive level on held-out contests by searching over many candidate programs.
importance: It demonstrates the interaction of generation scale, execution filters and selection in achieving code-task performance.
relevance: The manuscript's conclusions about persistence require compute-matched baselines: extra attempts can help when selection is informative.
transferable_idea: Compare sequential revision with independent candidate search under the same token and execution budget, using a separately validated selector.
limitations: Competitive-programming performance is not security repair, and large candidate budgets can hide weak individual-sample reliability or imperfect filtering.

title: Cybench: A Framework for Evaluating Cybersecurity Capabilities and Risks of Language Models
authors: Andy K. Zhang; Neil Perry; Riya Dulepet; Joey Ji; Celeste Menders; Justin W. Lin; Eliot Jones; Gashon Hussein; Samantha Liu; Donovan Jasper; Pura Peetathawatchai; Ari Glenn; Vikram Sivashankar; Daniel Zamoshchin; Leo Glikbarg; Derek Askaryar; Mike Yang; Teddy Zhang; Rishi Alluri; Nathan Tran; Rinnara Sangpisit; Polycarpos Yiorkadjis; Kenny Osele; Gautham Raghupathi; Dan Boneh; Daniel E. Ho; Percy Liang
source_note: arXiv author record identifies ICLR 2025.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Provides a reproducible benchmark of cybersecurity capture-the-flag challenges with executable environments and intermediate subgoals.
key_findings: The evaluated agents show substantial limitations, while subtask scaffolding helps expose which stages prevent completion.
importance: It offers a bridge from small synthetic security tasks to richer executable security environments.
relevance: The manuscript should test whether its feedback mechanism persists when agents must discover files, tools and exploit conditions.
transferable_idea: Select a small number of auditable tasks with independent replayable security outcomes and annotate progress before and after feedback interventions.
limitations: Offensive challenge completion is different from secure repair; CTF flags and challenge design do not certify defense quality or real-world deployment safety.

title: CyberGym: Evaluating AI Agents' Real-World Cybersecurity Capabilities at Scale
authors: Zhun Wang; Tianneng Shi; Jingxuan He; Matthew Cai; Jialin Zhang; Dawn Song
source_note: ICLR 2026 primary OpenReview PDF verified; use current published title rather than older preprint title.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Builds a large executable cybersecurity benchmark from real vulnerable software and evaluates agents on producing vulnerability-revealing inputs.
key_findings: The study reports successful reproduction on some real targets and discovery of additional defects during evaluation.
importance: It supplies concrete security outcomes linked to actual software, beyond source-token heuristics.
relevance: The manuscript's strongest external validity test would pair proposed patches with independently replayed attack inputs and benign functionality checks.
transferable_idea: Use reproducible proof-of-concept inputs to measure whether a misleading verdict causes a previously blocked attack to become effective again.
limitations: Attack reproduction and patch completeness are different objectives; absence of a reproduced exploit does not prove that a patch is secure.

title: AppWorld: A Controllable World of Apps and People for Benchmarking Interactive Coding Agents
authors: Harsh Trivedi; Tushar Khot; Mareike Hartmann; Ruskin Manku; Vinty Dong; Edward Li; Shashank Gupta; Ashish Sabharwal; Niranjan Balasubramanian
source_note: ACL 2024 proceedings verified; arXiv describes camera-ready version.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Creates a controllable ecosystem of simulated applications, users and APIs for evaluating interactive coding agents.
key_findings: Tasks are evaluated through state changes and collateral effects; the benchmark reveals difficulty even for strong agents.
importance: It treats satisfying the request and preserving unrelated desirable state as joint requirements.
relevance: The manuscript's overblocking cases likewise show that denying every request can appear secure while violating the legitimate task.
transferable_idea: Represent security and utility as separate invariants, then require both across the trajectory rather than only at the final verdict.
limitations: Simulated app tasks and authored assertions remain bounded specifications; their completeness must be audited before transferring conclusions.

title: AppWorld-UL: Benchmarking Diverse Agent-User Interactions for Tool-Use
authors: Junzhi Chen; Harsh Trivedi; Jane Pan; Michael JQ Zhang; Tejas Srinivasan; Niranjan Balasubramanian; Ashish Sabharwal
source_note: ICML 2026 PMLR volume 306, pages 16996–17023, independently confirms venue beyond the arXiv author comment.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Extends AppWorld with tasks requiring clarification, confirmation and communication about infeasible instructions.
key_findings: The 516-task benchmark reports that correct user interaction is essential and that compositional scenarios remain particularly difficult.
importance: It expands the decision space beyond acting versus stopping to include resolving ambiguity with a user.
relevance: The manuscript's stopping problem may sometimes be an evidence-acquisition or clarification problem rather than a binary abstention decision.
transferable_idea: Offer an explicit checker-disagreement escalation action and evaluate whether it preserves security without excessive deferral.
limitations: The user is simulated with specified knowledge boundaries; interaction quality and feasibility in real developer workflows require separate validation.

title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
authors: Edoardo Debenedetti; Jie Zhang; Mislav Balunović; Luca Beurer-Kellner; Marc Fischer; Florian Tramèr
source_note: NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks primary proceedings verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Provides a dynamic benchmark for tool-use agents exposed to prompt injections in untrusted data.
key_findings: The study evaluates both ordinary task utility and resilience to attacks, exposing tradeoffs across defenses and models.
importance: It makes the trust boundary between instructions and environmental content explicit.
relevance: The manuscript's misleading checker output can be studied as an environmental reliability problem while remaining distinct from malicious prompt injection.
transferable_idea: Label evidence sources and authority, compare accidental and adversarial verdict corruption, and score security together with legitimate task completion.
limitations: Injection defenses do not automatically protect against a semantically wrong but correctly formatted trusted checker; that distinction needs experimental isolation.
